analysis.one_liner: Bans hydraulic fracturing on public lands leased for oil and gas drilling.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban fracking on federal public lands never left committee: it died after a subcommittee referral, with no vote ever taken in the House.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Mineral Leasing Act to prohibit any company holding a federal public-lands lease from using hydraulic fracturing — fracking — on that land. It would apply only to new leases or renewed ones, so existing leases could continue until they were renewed or adjusted. The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, then to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, and never received a hearing or vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near federal public lands, use them for recreation, or drink water from areas overlying federal oil and gas leases. Roughly one in five Americans' water supplies cross lands managed for oil and gas development; a fracking ban would reduce the risk of chemical-laden drilling fluid contaminating groundwater, air pollution from well sites, and industrial disruption of parks, forests, and wildlife areas. It would also cut a source of greenhouse gas emissions, which benefits the public broadly.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits fracking on federal lands by adding a provision to the Mineral Leasing Act barring lessees from conducting hydraulic fracturing under any federal lease [S2][S3].
Applies to new, renewed, or readjusted leases, so future federal leasing could no longer include fracking while existing leases run out their terms [S2][S3].
Excludes conventional enhanced recovery methods like water flooding from the ban, targeting only the high-pressure fracturing technique [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies holding or seeking federal leases, which would lose access to a fracking-based extraction method on public land. Some consumers could see slightly higher energy prices if federal supply tightens, and some federal-lease royalty revenue flowing to the Treasury and states would be at risk where companies chose not to develop without fracking.

drawbacks.text: The ban would reduce domestic oil and gas production from federal lands, which could raise energy costs and reduce royalty revenues that fund the Treasury and Western states [S2][S3].
Applying the ban only at lease renewal means existing fracking under current leases would continue for years, so near-term environmental protection would be limited [S3].
The bill imposes the ban by statute rather than through site-by-site environmental review, without an exemption mechanism for cases where a regulator found fracking safe in a particular formation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit — keeping fracking off land owned by all Americans — is broad but diffuse, while its cost falls on a concentrated industry and modestly on federal revenue. The phase-in at lease renewal softens the economic disruption but also delays most of the environmental benefit. Whether the trade is worth it depends largely on how much weight one gives to groundwater and climate risk versus energy supply; the record contains no cost-benefit analysis.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Natural Resources Committee and its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee for the rest of the Congress and never got a hearing or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Pocan introduced the bill on April 21, 2015, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources [S1][S5].
On May 19, 2015, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, where it remained for the rest of the 114th Congress [S5].
The bill never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or action in the Senate, and expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies with federal leases are better off: fracking on public lands continued throughout the 114th Congress and beyond, and no restrictions from this bill ever took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies with federal leases

for.name: Rep. Mark Pocan
for.role: Sponsor, House Natural Resources Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban fracking on federal public lands.

for.name: 38 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Schakowsky, Grijalva, Nadler, and McGovern.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup after referring it to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: Faced losing fracking access on federal lands and opposed federal fracking restrictions during this period.

sides.party_line_note: All 39 initial sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill received no Republican support; it also never advanced far enough to test whether any Republicans would vote for it.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal land
industries.note: The bill would bar fracking under federal leases, removing access to a technique many companies use on public lands. Its interest in continuing fracking on public land runs against the public interest in protecting shared groundwater and landscapes from the practice's documented risks.

industries.industry: Oilfield services and hydraulic fracturing contractors
industries.note: Companies that perform fracking operations would lose federal-land work if the ban took effect. The loss would be gradual, since the bill applies only at lease renewal.
